title: Memory and the clock
summary: Make two gates remember a bit, catch a value on the clock's tick, then build a counter and push its clock until it breaks.

links.why: the same gates, now wired back into themselves
a processor's registers and pipeline stages are flip-flops on one clock
the slowest path between flip-flops sets the clock speed
links.if: a path between two registers gets longer
links.then: the whole processor must run at a slower clock, or the path is split into pipeline stages

ideas.how: smaller gates made clocks faster until about 2005; since then power, not gate delay, sets the limit
flip-flops in registers are the closest, fastest memory a processor has

tradeoffs.how: a faster clock needs shorter paths between flip-flops, and every tick costs energy

then: The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004, ticks 740 thousand times a second.
Desktop processors pass tens of millions of ticks a second as transistors shrink.
Processors reach one billion ticks a second (1 GHz).
Clock speeds stop climbing near 4 GHz: faster ticks would make too much heat, so chips add cores instead.
The fastest processors briefly reach about 6 GHz; most chips run far slower to save energy.

challenges.title: One bit of memory
challenges.task: Store a 1 in two NOR gates, let go, and watch it stay. Then set and reset at once.

challenges.title: One slot is enough
challenges.task: Make a flip-flop store a 1 with its input at 1 for only one time slot.

challenges.title: Find the speed limit
challenges.task: Run the counter as fast as it can go without a wrong count, at two different processes.

learn.plain: A gate on its own forgets: change its inputs and the old answer is gone. Wire two gates in a loop and each keeps the other's answer alive, like two people who keep reminding each other of a phone number. That loop is one bit of memory. A clock is a steady tick that tells every memory bit in the chip when to take its next value, so all the parts move in step, like rowers following a drum. The clock can only tick as fast as the slowest calculation between two ticks.
learn.engineer: A cross-coupled NOR pair is an SR latch; gating S and R with an enable gives a D latch, transparent while enabled; two latches on opposite clock phases make an edge-triggered master-slave D flip-flop. Synchronous design: every register samples on the same edge, and the minimum period is t_clk-to-Q + t_logic(max) + t_setup (plus clock skew and margin); hold time constrains the shortest path. The simulator here is event-driven with fixed gate delays from the studio's cell library, transport delays, and X for unknown; it leaves out wire delay, slew and load dependence, clock skew, PVT corners and metastability resolution. Real designs use static timing analysis rather than simulation to prove every path fits.

quiz.q: What makes two NOR gates remember a bit?
options: Each gate's output feeds the other's input, so they hold each other's value
quiz.why: The loop is the memory: with S and R both 0, each gate keeps the other in place.

quiz.q: A latch and a flip-flop share the same clock. D changes while the clock is 1. What happens?
options: The latch's output follows D; the flip-flop waits for the next rising edge
The flip-flop changes; the latch waits
quiz.why: A latch is transparent while its clock is 1; a flip-flop samples D only at the rising edge.

quiz.q: What sets a chip's top clock speed?
options: The slowest path between two flip-flops, plus their own delays
quiz.why: Each tick must leave time for a value to leave one flip-flop, pass the slowest logic and settle before the next flip-flop samples it.
